title: Common questions
excerpt: Most everyday work can start from the Hub’s templates and guides.
keywords: Most everyday work can start from the Hub’s templates and guides. For anything else, from a quick question to a larger project such as new design, video or animation, print, events or business cards, contact the Comms helpdesk. Say what you need, who it’s for and when you need it, and attach anything you already have. Open the Comms helpdesk Where are templates and slides? Slide templates and decks are under Presentations, and letterheads, memos and posters under Documents. All files lists every file, by section or newest first. Where are photos and video? In the staff media library in Canto. Photos and video shows a selection and links to it. Check each asset’s credit and permitted use. Can I adapt material myself? Yes, within its usage notes, and keep the credits. Ask the content owner before changing facts or meaning, and the creative team before substantial design changes. Why can I browse but not upload? Browsing and contributing have separate permissions. To add material, see Sharing your work below. Is my request booked once I send it? Not yet. The team replies to agree what will be made and when; a date isn’t fixed until then. If it’s urgent, say why and what could be cut back. Who approves the work? Name the content owner and the final reviewer in your request. The approval route depends on the work, so confirm it rather than assume it. Something is missing, wrong or broken Send the page link, what happened or what should change, and where the correct information comes from, to the Comms helpdesk. Sharing your work Sharing starts a review: nothing is published until its owner has checked it. How do I share a deck for others to reuse? Send the editable deck, or a link to it, through the Comms helpdesk, with its audience, event date, content owner and any limits on reuse. Once Communications has approved it, it can join Approved slide decks. How do I share photos or video? Ask the Comms helpdesk for an upload link; the Canto library is for browsing, not uploading. Include a title, who took it, where, and any rights or consent information. Keep working files where they are, so a new copy doesn’t become a competing version.

Sizes vary between conferences, so check rather than assume. Start from an SKAO poster template The poster templates come in A0, A1 and A2, with the logo, colours and text styles already set. Pick the one that matches the organiser’s size. Lead with one clear message Decide the main point first and let the title say it. Add the authors and affiliations, and keep the text short enough to read from a step or two away. Make it easy to follow Use clear headings and a reading order that runs naturally down the page. Give figures room to breathe, and keep the credit and source with every image and chart. Export and proof at full size Export a PDF and check it at 100% zoom: images should still look sharp at the printed size. Read it through once more for names, figures and spelling. title: Prepare files for print
excerpt: Every supplier and product is a little different, so set up and export your file to the supplier’s specification rather than a one-size-fits-all setting.
keywords: Before supplier handoff Every supplier and product is a little different, so set up and export your file to the supplier’s specification rather than a one-size-fits-all setting. Get the supplier’s specification first Ask for the finished size, the bleed and safe area, the colour profile and the PDF standard they accept. If anything is missing from the quote, ask before you export. Set up bleed and safe area Extend backgrounds and images past the trim by the bleed the supplier asks for, and keep text and logos inside the safe area so nothing important is trimmed off. Check colour and images Use the colour profile the supplier gives you and make sure images are sharp at the printed size. Spot colours, foils and other special finishes need setting up exactly as the supplier describes. Export and check the PDF Export to the supplier’s PDF standard with fonts embedded. Then check the PDF itself, not just your design file: text, page order, size and image quality. Get sign-off before it goes Make sure the content owner has approved the final artwork, and agree the proof, quantity, deadline and delivery details with the supplier. Not sure about a setting? Send the supplier’s specification and your draft to the Comms helpdesk. title: Accessibility checks
excerpt: Accessible work is easier for everyone to read. Build it in as you go, then check the file you actually share.
keywords: Make the work usable Accessible work is easier for everyone to read. Build it in as you go, then check the file you actually share. Use real headings and clear links Use the template’s heading styles rather than bold text, and write links that say where they go. Screen readers rely on both to find their way around. Describe images that carry meaning Give informative images alternative text that explains what they show and why they’re there. Purely decorative images should be marked as decorative so they’re skipped. Caption video and transcribe audio Add captions to video and offer a text version of any audio, so the content works with the sound off. Make text easy to read Check contrast: WCAG’s minimum is generally 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Don’t rely on colour alone; add labels, symbols or patterns too. Check the file you share Accessibility can be lost on export, so check the PDF or published version too: reading order, alternative text, and keyboard access and visible focus for anything interactive. The full standard These checks are a starting point, not a claim that the work passes a full accessibility audit. The standard itself has every requirement. WCAG 2.2 quick reference Every requirement in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, with techniques for meeting each one.
